name: Vulcan Salute
baseMeaning: A drawing of a hand held up with the palm forward, fingers split between two and three, used as signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting.
tldr: 🖖 Vulcan Salute: signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: On iOS the Vulcan Salute 🖖 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🖖 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the hand-gesture section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like answering a salute someone else started.

On Instagram 🖖 usually arrives as the tail of a caption rather than as a post of its own — a sign-off that reads as signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting under a photo, or a reaction somebody left on a story.

In TikTok comments 🖖 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🖖 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🖖 to do the work of signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting.

Millennials tend to send 🖖 deliberately, usually for something like answering a salute someone else started, and they read signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🖖 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🖖 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting subtext in it.

seoTitle: 🖖 Vulcan Salute Emoji Meaning - What Does 🖖 Really Mean?
seoDescription: What the vulcan salute emoji 🖖 means in text: signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting. Includes the misread it invites (sent by people with no connection to Star Trek at all, as a generic "live long and prosper" sign-off, which is why it can read as obscure rather than as a reference) and how to reply.

longForm.overview:
🖖 is the vulcan salute: a hand held up with the palm forward, fingers split between two and three. It arrived in Unicode 7.0, and it lives in the hand-gesture part of the emoji set, where the drawing is doing one specific job. Somebody sends it, and the picture either stands in for a sentence or stands in for a mood. Which one it is depends on what is around it.

At the plain level the gesture reads as signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, which is why it lands faster than a sentence would have landed.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets sent by people with no connection to Star Trek at all, as a generic "live long and prosper" sign-off, which is why it can read as obscure rather than as a reference. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🖐️ Raised Hand: the plain raised hand reads as a stop or high five, the split fingers mark the salute. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The drawing on this page is the neutral one. The same vulcan salute exists in five skin tones, and each of those pages covers how a particular tone gets read by the people who send it. The gesture does not change between them; what changes is who it looks like it is coming from.

Practically, this is what the page is for: what the vulcan salute emoji is used for, how it behaves in the places people actually use it, and where the drawing is more confident than the person who sent it. The two jobs it does most often are signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish and answering a salute someone else started, and the sections below break both of them down.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The first job 🖖 does is signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish. It gets typed at the end of a sentence that already made the point, and it removes the need to explain how the sender wants the message taken. Nobody has to write "you know what I mean", because the picture says it.

The second is answering a salute someone else started. Here the emoji is doing something different: it is not the punchline, it is the tone. The message could have been sent without it, but it would have read as flat.

Where the gesture lands depends on the room. In a family thread 🖖 is closer to a sign-off, in a work channel it is a decision or a handover, and in a dating thread it is a way of making a small joke without writing one. The same drawing moves because the people reading it expect different things.

That is also why the skin-tone versions matter. The five variants under this family cover the same gesture, and the tone you pick says something about you before the sentence is read.

The habit worth naming is the one where the emoji replaces a reply altogether. Somebody asks a question, and 🖖 goes back on its own. It reads as "signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting", and it saves the sender a sentence — which is exactly why it is so easy to send something that means less than intended.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Do not use 🖖 when you mean 🖐️ Raised Hand. The plain raised hand reads as a stop or high five, the split fingers mark the salute. The two drawings are easy to confuse, and the wrong one changes the message from one thing to a different thing entirely.

And do not use it as a reaction to somebody who is upset. A bare 🖖 in a thread about a person reads as "signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting", which is about the picture and not about them.

Skip it when the sentence underneath it is the important part. The emoji gets sent by people with no connection to Star Trek at all, as a generic "live long and prosper" sign-off, which is why it can read as obscure rather than as a reference. Once that happens the emoji is carrying the message, and the message has drifted somewhere neither sender intended.

It is also a poor choice in a first exchange with somebody you do not know. There is no warmth baked into the drawing, and vulcan salute gestures often collect a slightly superior edge from being used as answers to other people's messages.

Finally, leave it out of formal settings where the tone is supposed to be neutral. 🖖 in a thread about somebody's performance, or in a message to a client you have never met, buys very little and risks a read of signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting as arrogance.
longForm.howToReply:
The easy reply is to match it with the same 🖖. That confirms the tone without adding anything, and it works when the original message was a reaction rather than a question.

If the vulcan salute was aimed at you — a nudge, a handover, a request for a decision — answer in words. A gesture answering a gesture leaves the actual point unanswered.

If somebody sends it and you are not sure what register they are in, respond to the sentence rather than to the emoji. The drawing gets sent by people with no connection to Star Trek at all, as a generic "live long and prosper" sign-off, which is why it can read as obscure rather than as a reference — and the sentence is the part that tells you which reading you are dealing with.

And when you want the warmth without the ambiguity, add a line of text. A message like signing off a message with a sci-fi flourish almost always needs the sentence, because the picture on its own leaves the reader to guess whether you meant signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting or something sharper.

faqs.question: What does 🖖 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🖖 is used for signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting. The drawing shows a hand held up with the palm forward, fingers split between two and three, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🖖 and 🖐️?
faqs.answer: The plain raised hand reads as a stop or high five, the split fingers mark the salute. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🖖 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as signalling a Star Trek salute or sci-fi greeting, but it gets sent by people with no connection to Star Trek at all, as a generic "live long and prosper" sign-off, which is why it can read as obscure rather than as a reference. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🖖 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🖖 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under vulcan salute show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.
